nameStory: The Yellow Specklebelly gets its charming name from the distinctive pale yellow spots scattered across its underside, which looks just like a speckled belly when you flip it over! These whitish-yellow spots are actually tiny breathing pores called pseudocyphellae, which inspired both the common name and the scientific genus name Pseudocyphellaria.
description: Yellow Specklebelly is a large, leafy lichen that forms impressive rosettes on tree bark and rocks in cool, moist forests. This foliose lichen can grow quite large, with individual lobes reaching 4-6 inches across and entire colonies sometimes spanning over a foot wide. The upper surface is typically brownish-gray to olive-brown when dry, turning a rich green when wet, while the underside reveals the telltale yellow speckles that give this lichen its name.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: The underside shows distinctive whitish-yellow spots (pseudocyphellae) scattered across a dark brown to black background - like freckles on dark skin

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Large, leafy lobes that feel somewhat leathery and flexible when moist, becoming more brittle when completely dry

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Upper surface shifts dramatically from dull brownish-gray when dry to vibrant green when wet - the transformation happens within minutes of rain

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: One of the larger lichens you'll encounter, with individual lobes 2-6 inches long and colonies that can cover significant portions of tree trunks

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on bark of deciduous trees, especially maples and birches, in areas with consistently high humidity

habitat: Yellow Specklebelly thrives in cool, humid forests throughout New England's mountains and northern regions, particularly in areas with frequent fog or mist. You'll find it growing on the bark of mature deciduous trees like sugar maple, yellow birch, and American beech, typically on the north-facing sides where moisture lingers longest. It prefers elevations above 1,000 feet where the air stays consistently moist.

seasonality.spring: The lichen appears most vibrant in spring as frequent rains keep it green and pliable. This is an excellent time to see the dramatic color change from brown to green as moisture activates photosynthesis.
seasonality.summer: During dry summer periods, Yellow Specklebelly becomes dormant and brownish-gray, but summer storms quickly revive its green color. The contrast between wet and dry appearance is most dramatic in summer.
seasonality.fall: Autumn's frequent rains and morning dew keep the lichen active and green for extended periods. The yellow speckles on the underside are often most visible now as the lichen stays moist and flexible.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible year-round, though often dormant and brown-colored during dry winter periods. Snow melt and winter thaws can briefly activate the green coloration even in cold weather.

funFact: Yellow Specklebelly can survive being completely dried out for months, losing up to 95% of its water content, then spring back to life and resume photosynthesis within 30 minutes of getting wet - faster than most plants can even absorb water through their roots!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Lung Lichen, which also grows large and leafy on trees, but Lung Lichen has a distinctive network of ridges on top (like lung tissue) and lacks the yellow speckles underneath. Remember: speckles = Specklebelly, ridges = Lung Lichen.
contextualKnowledge: **Uncertain claim flagged**: Yellow Specklebelly is quite rare in New England with only 14 recorded observations, so you're looking at a real treasure if you find one! This lichen is considered an indicator of old-growth forest conditions and excellent air quality, making it increasingly uncommon in our region.
compareHints: Since Yellow Specklebelly is the only member of its genus in New England, compare it with other large foliose lichens in the Lobariaceae family like Lung Lichen. Yellow Specklebelly is distinguished by its smooth upper surface (versus ridged) and especially by those characteristic yellow pseudocyphellae on the underside. Most other large leafy lichens in our region either lack these spots entirely or have white spots instead of yellow ones.
